Śrīṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ aiṃ vajravailocanīye hrīṃ hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā.
The mantra of Chinnamastā.
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ, obeisance to Mahālakṣmī.
Oṃ hrīṃ Bagalāmukhī! Paralyze the speech and mouths of all the wicked; nail down their tongues; destroy their intellect! Hrīṃ oṃ svāhā!
Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hauṃ Kāli (2) Mahākāli kili (2) Mahābhairavi Caṇḍike svāhā.
Hrūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ, svāhā to Dakṣiṇakālikā!
Aiṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ triṃ svāhā. To Nakṣatrayā.
aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ hsphreṃ hsauṃ lāṃ krīṃ śrīṃ śsrāṃ, obeisance to Svacchandeśvara, pā pū (5).
By means of her who moves with playful freedom.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hsphreṃ Hsauṃ Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Hrūṃ, [obeisance] to Aghoreśvara Bhairava, Pā Pū (5).
According to the Bhairavasvacchanda.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hsphreṃ Hsauṃ Kṣmhrāṃ Kṣmhrīṃ Kṣmhrūṃ, to Prapañceśvara Ādibhairava, Pā Pū (5). To Śrī Saṃvartā.
Āṃ hūṃ phaṭ, svāhā to Vajrayoginī!
Oṃ lvryhrīṃ, obeisance to Trailokyavijayā. Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ hsauṃ, obeisance, O Blessed One, O Sovereign Annapūrṇeśvarī; grant me my desired object, svāhā! [This is for] Annapūrṇā.
The meditation on Gaurī.
One should always worship that Gaurī, who possesses a golden luster, holding a mirror and a vessel of collyrium in her [left] arms, and a noose and a goad in her right arms.
The flower of meditative concentration (2). The triple añjali gesture (3).
Hrīṃ Gaurī Rudradayite Yogeśvarī Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā. Thus is the bali offering.
Thus ends the Gaurīyā.
O Garuda, cast it away, svāhā!
Then follows the purification of the garland; having sipped water according to the triple reality (tritatva).
Salutation to the Guru, Gaṇeśa, and the chosen deity; [this is] the pranayama and the twenty-eight nyāsas.
Purification of the Water: For the purpose of bathing in water, one should recite the *mālā-mantra*:
Oṃ kṣaṃ laṃ haṃ saṃ ṣaṃ śaṃ vaṃ laṃ raṃ yaṃ maṃ bhaṃ baṃ phaṃ paṃ naṃ dhaṃ daṃ thaṃ taṃ ṇaṃ ḍhaṃ ḍaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭaṃ ñaṃ jhaṃ jaṃ chaṃ.
caṃ ṅaṃ ghaṃ gaṃ khaṃ kaṃ aḥ aṃ auṃ oṃ aiṃ eṃ ḹṃ ḷṃ ṝṃ ṛṃ ūṃ uṃ īṃ iṃ āṃ aṃ ||
One should not recite the *thva* mantra; [one should perform] the bathing with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Recite the root mantra *haṃ* (nine times), *saṃ* (nine times), and *dhāra* (one hundred and eight times).
Then, the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).
Aiṁ (5) Āṁ Hrīṁ Kroṁ Haṃ So: Here are the vital breaths of the venerable Kubjikāmālā.
Aiṃ (5) Āṃ Hrīṃ Kroṃ Haṃ So; O life-force of the venerable Kubjikāmālā, remain here!
Aiṃ (5) Āṃ Hrīṃ Kroṃ Haṃ So. O Śrī Kubjikāmālā, here [are] all the senses.
Aiṃ (5) Āṃ Hrīṃ Kroṃ Haṃ So! O Speech, Mind, Eyes, Ears, Tongue, Nose, and Vital Breath of the venerable Kubjikāmālā, may all the senses come here and remain happily for a long time;
Svāhā! (3)
Thus it was said regarding the foot-washing water.
Aiṁ (5) Haṁ (9) Saṁ (9). Salutation to the venerable Kubjikāmālā; this is the water for the feet.

In this manner, the offering of the guest-water (argha), water for sipping (ācamana), bathing materials, sandalwood paste and so forth, as well as the presentation of incense, lamps, and food offerings (naivedya) [should be performed].
With the root mantra, [offer] three handfuls of flowers. Recitation and hymn of praise.
Thus ends the purification of the rosary.
In that regard, first comes the examination of the teacher and the disciple.
Peaceful, self-controlled, and dissolved [in meditation], she was humble and dressed in pure attire.
He was of pure conduct, highly renowned, clean, skillful, and possessed of excellent intelligence.
One who is most established in meditation, skilled in mantra and tantra, and capable of both restraint and favor is always designated as a guru. This is the characteristic of a guru.
He is peaceful, disciplined, pure in soul, possessed of purity, capable of maintaining his vows,
competent, of noble birth, wise, of virtuous conduct, and wealthy.
One endowed with such qualities as these becomes a disciple, and not otherwise. This is the definition of a disciple.
Then follows the worship of the conch shell.
(5) The moon disk and so forth, the five hungry ghosts and so forth.
Aiṃ (5) mrāṃ mrīṃ mrīṃ, O you who whirl with the conch-blowing! (2) mrāṃ mrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.

Aiṃ (5) Haṃ (9) || Vatiśi || (5) Aghorāya Pā Pū (5) || (5) To the Supreme Aghora, to the one of terrible form, to the one with a terrible face, to the Fierce, to the Terrifying, to the one who vomits, to the one who drinks, to the one who causes drinking. The worship of the six limbs.

The invocation of the cow, the offering of the terrible weapon (*ghorāstra*), the recitation (*japa*) with the root mantra and the conch, the incense, the lamp, the hymn (*stotra*), and the *Śyāmā*— these constitute the complete worship (*saṃpūjā*).
Then, on the Mahānavamī day, the Āgama arrived, purified by the ritual sprinkling.
The ritual procedure for Navarātra.

The placement (*nyāsa*) of the sharp latent impressions (*patuvāsana*), performed according to the prescribed ritual at the gateway of the city of death (*mārakoca-tāyahāra*). *Nyāsa:* [End of section]
Phaṭ! To the one who bestows the crown of the limbs of the gods! Phitaya! To the one whose form is triangular!
Tha-tha-pu-vā-sa-na-co-yaṃ-tra-aṃ-ga-si-ra-tha-ne-mā-ra phaṭ | Sā-ma phaṭ | Sā-ma-mā-ra ||
Here is the formula: "I offer oblations; may there be a favorable moment. O Chanda, root of the foremost mantras."
Śrīsaṃvartā || Saṃvartā was born from the womb of Laṅkhavī by means of a mantra.

The pressing of the *siṃdhra* oil-press and the application of sandalwood paste and so forth; the offering of food to the crows and the application of *mālaka* and sandalwood paste—all these are concluded. Now follows the worship of the deity according to the prescribed rule; the procedure for installation is essential.
The Mahānavamī [rite] according to the prescribed rule, the propitiation with animals, the sword [rite], and the Komaṛī sacrifice.
The wheel of the pledge is like the doctrine of the Kalaṅka-crow; Cāmuṇḍā shakes it off as if it were the gratification of beasts.
A garland.
Then follows the wandering mendicant (cāraṇa): the ritual procedure for the worship of the deity is as before, up to the recitation of mantras and hymns at the swing.
The dissolution of the samaya and so forth, the withdrawal [of the deity], the offering of libations (tarpaṇa), the dismissal of the weapon-mantra, and the release of the hands.

With the *mohani* weapon, the discharge of the cord; for the deity, it is the breaking of all [impurities], like the shadow of a jar, with the cord and the *mohani*. With the weapon, the discharge at the end of the nine nights; for the deity, it is the breaking of all [impurities], like the shadow.
The propitiation with their respective mantras is performed for the deity; [this concludes] the single or multiple blessings of the deities.

Then, having placed the sacrificial wife upon the *svastika* with the *śakti* mantra, and having caused the deity to face [the sacrificer], [the officiant] should offer the oblation for the sacrificer with the *jūr-asā* mantra;
then, with the *jūr-asā* mantra, he should perform the *āvahana* (invocation) for the sacrificer. Then, with the *vah-ava-pra-hna-saka-nate* mantra, [he should perform the invocation].
The vase-consecration (kalaśābhiṣeka) with its qualities and enchantments, the sandalwood and flowers, the blessings, the entire Mālakoṣṭha,
the Nidhura sages, the sacrificer (yajamāna), the power of the juices, the jar of space—
having offered all these, the Yogeshī remains in the world.

Upon the completion of the pot-offering (kumbha-havana), there is the self-revelation (svayadarśana) which transcends all castes. He should bestow upon everyone this thousand-fold essence of the Vāruṇīs. This includes the self-essence, the satisfaction through affection, the libation for the deceased (pretatarpaṇa), and the formal acceptance.
Having drawn seven mandalas upon the tips of the eight petals, representing the movement toward the directions and the purification of the directions.
The offerings to Pañcabali, Tribali, Yoginībali, Cāmuṇḍābali, and Kṣetramahākālabali, and the ritual dismissal (visarjana).

The dismissal of the primary sword: *kuṣmāṇḍa phaṭ semaṇḍalasate*. In the formula for dismissal, [the word] "Durgā Devī" is used; for the formula regarding the sword, "Mārkaṇḍeya" is used. Holding a fruit and a book in the left hand and holding a sword in the right, he utters the words of departure, "Victory! (vijayaṃ), while facing the north. In that maṇḍala...

Having gone to the maṇḍala, for the purpose of severing the Kuṣmāṇḍas, through the speech of the Asamata-paścimaja-jeṣṭhāja-jeṣṭhāmnāya, and for the sake of the destruction of enemies, the attainment of the sword (*khaḍgasiddhi*), and the desire for victory, [this is offered] to the venerable Lord Śrī Kubjikā. Śrī...
The worship of the goddess Ugracaṇḍā is complete; I destroy such-and-such an enemy for Kuṣmāṇḍa. (3)

Thus, having returned to the mandala once more, it is complete. Then, one should maintain the primary seat, beginning with the root [mantra]. The vessel and the attendant are placed; it is established and witnessed by the Sun.
Likewise, in the temples of the gods, one should recite the mantra along with the *vidyā-cakra*. The statement is: "O Goddess Durgā, Mother of the World!"
The polishing of the mirror; the offering of bali should be cast in its proper place; the feast for those bound by the pledge (samaya-bhojya).
Thus, these noble ones, through their arrival and protection, have brought about this for him.
During the ritual of satisfying the deities with the sword-sacrifice, one should drink [the offering];
then, by means of that, one should perform the meditation on the deities of the six traditions (ṣaḍāmnāya).

Aiṁ Hrīṁ Kṣhphrīṁ! [I bow to the one] who has the luster of a sapphire, is adorned with ten long arms, whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and who is beautiful, holding a trident and a skull-cup.
In his lotus-like hands, he holds a hand-drum, a rosary, and a spear;
he is beautifully adorned, with a sugarcane bow, an arrow, and a sword in his grasp.
One should meditate upon Pūrṇeśī, whose limbs are adorned with all ornaments.
The mantra is: Ū. [This belongs to] the Eastern Tradition; the Southern Tradition.

Aiṃ Hrīṃ Khhsphreṃ! She who resembles a thousand suns, blazing with youth, possessing six arms, and raised in the gestures of the noose, the goad, the skull-cup, and the granting of boons and fearlessness; she who is joyful, surrounded by the powers of the Siddhas and the Moon.
Adorned with every ornament, she is the sovereign of night, the supreme goddess.
Mantra: Ūḥ.
The Western Tradition.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hsphreṃ Hsauṃ: [I meditate upon] the one who has the luster of the sky, three eyes, seated upon the body of a bull, clad in silk garments, with a smiling face,
and holding in his single pair of arms a hand-drum, an axe, and vajras at the tips of his [other] mandalas.

Holding a conch, a skull-topped staff, a noose, a goad, a shield, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a sword, a trident, a bow, a bell, and a skull-cup; with matted hair and wearing the crescent moon, she plays the lute.
Resembling the rising sun, seated upon the back of a lion, her body bent by the weight of her breasts,
beautiful with all ornaments,
with hands granting fearlessness and boons, possessing one face and three eyes, her lotus-face radiant with joy.
I meditate upon Kubjikā.
Mantra: Oṃ.
The Uttara-Āmnāya.
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Phreṃ! O Mahākālī of blue complexion, with three faces and nine eyes;
your right face is yellow, and the northern one is like fire.
Her eyes are fixed upon the maṇḍala; she possesses eight arms and a slender body;
her mass of matted hair is tawny and stands upright, and she has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
Adorned with twenty-seven ornaments including blood-stained earrings, she is enriched by the beauty of bone-earrings and wears a garland of skulls upon her head.
Adorned with tinkling girdles, anklets, and excellent small bells,
she is mounted upon a corpse of Śiva, with streams of blood flowing from her mouth.
Indra and the others, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva,
are the makers of yellow, black, dark-blue, red, smoke-colored, and white appearances respectively.
Holding a vajra, staff, spear, discus, trident, and khaṭvāṅga,
with their index fingers placed in their mouths, they stand below Śiva, each possessing three eyes.
The goddess sits firmly in the lotus posture (padmāsana), with full and elevated breasts;
in her left hand she holds a skull-cup (kapāla) filled with blood, which is exceedingly beautiful.
Holding a trident with sound in her right hand,
she likewise holds a vajra, a goad, and a mallet in her right hands.
In her left [hands] she holds a noose, a khaṭvāṅga staff, and a corpse;
she dwells in the midst of the subtle vibration of consciousness (citkalā), and is solely of the nature of light.
One should meditate upon this embodied Great Goddess with nine faces, who bestows the state of Nirvāṇa and whose sphere of activity transcends all existence.
One should worship the thirty-three-syllable [mantra] according to the distinction of the authority over enjoyments (bhogādhikāra).
This goddess is proclaimed to have nine faces in her supreme form (parārūpa).
The sixteen-syllable mantra is *uṃ*.
The Fortune of Accomplishment.

Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ! [I salute] the beautiful one whose nature is Brahman, who possesses the luster of the full moon and is as white as a conch or a jasmine flower; she is adorned with matted hair joined by a crescent moon and shines with fifteen eyes;
she is endowed with five faces above Rudra and holds a trident, a sword, a severed head, and a goad.
He holds a khaṭvāṅga, a bowl, a noose, and a flask in his hands, and displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The root garland mantra is: Oṃ.
The Upper Tradition (Ūrdhvāmnāya).
Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauṃḥ! I bow to the beautiful one who dwells upon the single seat composed of the sun, moon, and fire; who is as crimson as the rising morning sun;
whose crown is adorned with the crescent moon and three eyes; who possesses full breasts;
and who holds in her hands a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow, and a flower-arrow.
One should worship her, whose limbs are like young blossoms and who is adorned with various ornaments, during the lunar phase of the moon.
The mantra for the seed-syllable in the fourth state is *uṃ*. For the *adhāmnāya*: *aiṃ hrīṃ khphre* [is used] with the water-pot (*kalaśa*).
Aiṁ (5). The goddess Kuṇḍacandanasundarī beholds the Lord, who stands in the center of a lunar disc, as pure as clear crystal and resembling cow’s milk.
Four-armed and of great splendor, adorned with three eyes,
eternally wearing a mass of matted hair, and having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
Complete with all her garments and adorned with all ornaments;
in her left hand she holds a vessel of pure water, and in her right, a rosary of beads.
Holding a book and a lotus stalk in his hands, ever-radiant,
praised by all the best of gods, and clothed in divine garments.
One who desires great fortune should meditate upon that Mṛtyuñjaya-Bhairava, who pacifies all death and bestows the fruit of all accomplishments.
The mantra is: Um.
Aiṃ (5). The goddess Padmasiṃhāsanā is swift and possesses the crimson hue of the pomegranate;
the goddess resembles lac juice and has a radiance equal to that of a ruby.
She has one face and three eyes, is adorned with divine ornaments,
holds a sword and a shield in her hands, and carries a full vessel together with a drop.
Seated comfortably in the lotus posture, the embodiment of a gentle form—
having thus meditated upon the Great Goddess Vāruṇī, the Mistress of Kubjikā.
Mantra: Uṃ. Kumbhayā.
Belonging to Kaumārī.

Oṃ! To Kaumārī, the Mother of the Kula, who resembles a bandhūka flower, whose radiance is equal to ten million flashes of lightning, who has four arms and is seated upon a peacock—[the mantra is] Ūṃ. Thus is the visualization.
Oṃ, homage to the Guru! Now, for the sake of the mantra, the wise person should purify the months and so forth.
In Caitra, initiation leads to suffering; in Vaiśākha, there is an accumulation of jewels;
in Jyeṣṭha, death occurs; and in Āṣāḍha, there is the destruction of kinsmen.
Prosperity will surely come in the month of Śrāvaṇa, decline in Bhādrapada,
and for living beings, initiation in the month of Āśvina bestows all fruits.
In Kārttika there will be knowledge; in Mārgaśīrṣa it takes away wealth;
in Pauṣa there is the loss of knowledge; and in Māgha there is an increase in intelligence.
In the month of Phālguna, there is the attainment of all perfections; one should avoid the month of Āśvala.
As for the commencement of mantras, it should be done in Caitra for the sake of the supreme human goal.
The statement of Gautama refers specifically to the Vaiṣṇavas.
In that regard, it is stated in the Yāmala:
Failure, attainment of the stages, death, loss of kinsmen,
increase of lifespan, destruction of progeny, prosperity, and accumulation of jewels.

The results for the months beginning with Caitra are to be known as follows: full fruit, increase of enemies, intelligence, and the fulfillment of desires; one should avoid the intercalary month (malamāsa).
The rule regarding the days of the week.
On Sunday there will be suffering; on Monday it bestows peace;
Mars destroys longevity—one should avoid initiation on that day.
Under Mercury one attains beauty; under Jupiter, there shall be knowledge;
under Venus, one attains good fortune; and under Saturn, there is loss of cattle.
Now follows the rule regarding the lunar days (tithi).
The fourth, the ninth, as well as the fourteenth, the eighth;
the full moon day, the fifth, and likewise the second and the seventh.
The thirteenth and the tenth lunar days are praised as bestowing all accomplishments;
initiation is auspicious during the bright fortnight, and even during the dark fortnight, provided it is before the fifth day.
For those desiring liberation, [the initiation] should be performed during the dark fortnight; likewise, for those desiring land, during the bright fortnight.
On the eighth or the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the rite of initiation bestows auspiciousness.
As for that which is the Vaiṣṇava tantra:
On the second lunar day one becomes a practitioner; on the third, one becomes pure;
on the fourth, there will be loss of wealth; and on the fifth, there is an increase of intelligence.
On the sixth day, the destruction of knowledge and happiness may occur;
on the seventh day, there shall be loss of intellect; on the eighth, the destruction of the body occurs on the ninth.
On the tenth day there is royal fortune; on the eleventh, one becomes pure;
on the twelfth, all success shall be attained; and on the thirteenth, poverty occurs.
On the fourteenth day, one is born into the womb of an animal; at the end [of the fortnight], there is loss;
at the conclusion of the fortnight, there is an increase in merit, yet one should avoid Vedic study.
When there is the roar of thunder at twilight or an earthquake occurs at the time of death,
one should avoid those days declared in the Śruti as unfit for study (anadhyāya).
Thus indeed is the supreme state of the Vaiṣṇavas.
Now follows the rule regarding the lunar mansions.
In Aśvinī one attains happiness; in Bharaṇī death is certain;
in Kṛttikā one becomes miserable; and in Rohiṇī one becomes eloquent.
In Mṛgaśīrṣa there is the attainment of happiness; in Ārdrā, the destruction of kinsmen;
in Punarvasu, one becomes miserable; and in Puṣya, one becomes wealthy.
Under Āśleṣā one will become miserable; under Maghā one will meet with ruin;
and indeed, under both Phalgunīs, there will surely be an increase in cattle.
In Hasta there will be loss of wealth; in Citrā and Svātī one shall be happy;
in Viśākhā there is happiness, and in Anurādhā the destruction of kinsmen.
Under Jyeṣṭhā, there shall be an increase of sons; under Mūlā, an increase of fame;
and under Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā, both shall be bestowers of renown.
One will be miserable under Śravaṇā; poverty under Dhaniṣṭhā;
intelligence under Śatabhiṣā; and poverty under Pūrvabhādrapadā.
There is happiness under Uttarābhādrapadā, and an increase in fame under Revatī.
The rule for the ascendant.
One should carry out the commencement of initiation when the ascendants are Taurus, Leo, Virgo, Sagittarius, or Pisces, and when the moon and the stars are favorable.
The Moon situated in the third, eleventh, sixth,
or tenth house is declared auspicious as the birth-moon, provided it is not the natal asterism.
In the bright fortnight, the second, fifth, and ninth lunar days are auspicious;
even when conjoined with those houses that are pure in their planetary course, the Moon is favorable.
Even when situated between two auspicious [planets], the Moon will bestow auspicious results;
likewise on the third, seventh, sixteenth, and eighteenth lunar days.
One should avoid performing auspicious rites under the nineteenth, twentieth, twenty-third, and likewise the twenty-fifth lunar mansions.
In the Rudrayāmala.

On an auspicious day characterized by purity of the five factors, when the moon and stars are favorable, and during the rising of Jupiter and Venus, the performance of the ritual for the mantra is highly commended.
"Five times over."
The purpose of the calculation of the yoga is for the sake of determining the purity of the lunar days (tithis) and weekdays (vāras).
In the Vārāhī Tantra.
If Venus is in its eighth or its exaltation, or if Jupiter is in the eleventh house,
then no fault exists even if [the Moon] is in Aries, Scorpio, or Leo.

In this context, although even the pure month of Bhādrapada is prohibited, nevertheless, the mention of Bhādrapada is for the purpose of establishing its general status; it is merely a specific rule regarding initiation (*dīkṣā*), but [it applies] to all ritual actions (*sarvakarma*).
In the *Ratnāvalī*:
Yoga, Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya,
Śobhana, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Sukarman, Sādhya, Śukla, and Harṣaṇa.
Vāriyā, Anara, Siddha, Brahma, Aindra, and the sixteenth, Ṣoḍaśa—
these should be auspicious karaṇas, especially during initiation (dīkṣā).
One should specifically avoid the Śakuni and other such configurations, as well as the Adhiṣṭi yoga.
In the Yoginīhṛdaya.
Since that purification of the lunar day, the weekday, and so forth has been described by me previously,
the supreme mantra-initiation (mantradīkṣā) must be understood as distinct from that by the best of practitioners.
The initiation into knowledge (vidyādīkṣā) and the purification of the lunar day, month, and so forth,
as well as the initiation [itself], should be performed according to the Guru’s command whenever there is a desire for it.

During the equinoxes, the solstices, on the full moon of Āṣāḍha, during the Madana festival, at the time of initiation, and on the sacred festival of the Guru, one should diligently perform the rite of the Pavitra.
The rule regarding the festival of the Guru is in that very same place.
The sixth day in the month of Bhādrapada, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in Āśvina (Iṣa),
the ninth day of the bright fortnight in Kārttika, and the second day of the bright fortnight in Mārgaśīrṣa.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight in Pauṣa, the excellent fourth day in Māgha,
the ninth day of the bright fortnight in Phālguna, and the thirteenth day of Kāma (the bright fortnight) in Caitra.
In Vaiśākha, Akṣayā is praised; likewise, Daśaharā is in Jyeṣṭha;
the fifth day of the bright fortnight in Āṣāḍha, and the fifth day of the dark fortnight in Śrāvaṇa.
On these festival days of the Guru, one obtains the fruit of ten million sacred fords (tīrthas).
Even during censured months, initiation is declared auspicious during an eclipse.
There is nothing on earth equal to the time of a solar eclipse;
whatever action is performed then, one shall obtain infinite fruit therefrom.
In the Śaktiyāmala.
A lunar eclipse is equal to a thousand solar eclipses;
however, an eclipse occurring on one's own [natal] day is said to be a hundred-thousandfold more significant.
And in the Yoginīhṛdaya:
During the sun's transit into a zodiac sign and likewise during a solar eclipse,
one should never consider the ascendant or other such astrological factors at all.
Especially on the Great Eighth Day, one should thoroughly purify what is the proper time and what is not.
Thus ends the fruit of the lunar day of initiation.
If someone here has said that one should worship the unbroken lotus and sprinkle that water on the head with the hair alone eight times, [that is not so].
Having placed [the manuscript] within eight [vessels], one should recite it into the ear; this is the procedure for oral instruction.
[This should be done] during an eclipse of the moon or sun, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), in a field of accomplishment (siddhikṣetra), or in a temple of Śiva.
The mere proclamation of the mantra is called "instruction" (upadeśa).
Such is the instruction.
If one imparts the mantra at midnight on the fourteenth day, during an eclipse, or under the Aśvinī asterism,
that practitioner of mantra will remain poor for seven lifetimes.
The fourteenth lunar day joined with the new moon (Kuhū) is highly meritorious yet brings fear;
it must not be observed by a householder, for it takes away sons, grandsons, and wealth.

The Śivāghorā, the Antarā, the Pretā, and the Sāvitrī [observances] on the fourteenth day must be performed even when it coincides with the new moon (Kuhū); furthermore, the observance should be maintained on the new moon itself.
Auspicious.
